title: Why tell hard history
hookLine: the tradition is made of people, and people fail and endure

lines: THE BUDDHA ASKS THEM TO STOP.
cards: In the town of Kosambi, the monks are fighting. It started small, over whether one monk had broken a rule or not. Now the community has split in two.
They argue in the meeting hall. They argue in the village. The Buddha himself comes and asks them to stop, and, the texts say, they tell him, more or less, to leave it to them.

This is the Buddha's own community, in his own lifetime, kept and recited by the very tradition it embarrasses. Today opens a new stretch of the path: history held honestly. Why tell the hard parts at all?

teach.h: THE BUDDHA LEAVES FOR THE FOREST.
teach.b: The quarrel at Kosambi is told in the Vinaya and in the Majjhima Nikaya, and it doesn't end with a miracle. The Buddha tries to reconcile them.

Then he leaves, walking alone into the forest, and the texts describe him visiting a few monks living together in harmony, as if to see what a good community looks like. Then something ordinary happens back in Kosambi.
The lay followers, the people who feed the monks, decide that monks who won't make peace get neither their respect nor their alms. Hungry and embarrassed, the monks go and make it up.

The Dhammapada has a verse that tradition links to this quarrel. In Max Muller's translation: "The world does not know that we must all come to an end here;—but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once."
So here's one answer to today's question. The tradition tells hard history because its own texts do. The sangha, the community, is made of people.
People argue, get proud, misuse power, and also repair, apologize and endure. A story where the community never fails would be hard to believe, and harder to learn from.
Over the next days: kings who protected monks and kings who used them, persecutions, monks who spoke for war and monks who marched for peace.

teach.h: THE SANGHA IS MADE OF PEOPLE.
teach.b: None of it is told to score a point against Buddhists, and none of it is the whole picture. It's told the way Kosambi is told: plainly, with the failure and the repair side by side.

how: Buddhist monastics recite the Vinaya, which records the incidents behind its rules, including quarrels and misconduct, and Buddhist teachers and historians also discuss the community's failures openly alongside its achievements.

o: a meeting called to settle a dispute
a temple building where monks live
the Buddhist community, made of people

games.q: why tell hard history: tap the pairs.
p: the monks split into two sides
asked them to stop, then left

s: the scriptures hide the quarrels of the Buddha's own monks
the Kosambi quarrel is told in the Vinaya and the Majjhima Nikaya.
at Kosambi, lay followers helped end the quarrel
they withheld respect and alms from monks who wouldn't make peace.
the Buddha ended the quarrel with a miracle
he tried, then left for the forest; the monks made peace later.

games.q: you're the Buddha. the monks of Kosambi are split and won't stop quarreling, even when you ask them to. what do you do?
o: expel one side from the community.
keep arguing with them until they give in.
leave them and go alone into the forest.
games.why: he walks off alone into the forest. the quarrel ends later, after the lay followers stop supporting monks who won't make peace.

practice: Bring to mind a hard story from a group you belong to, a family, a team, a school, a faith, not the worst one, a medium one, and let it be true without arguing or defending anyone.
Notice where it lands in the body, the jaw, the chest, the stomach, and breathe into that place. Then, if you can, find one person in that story who tried to repair something, and hold both.

wordCard.voice: Sangha. The community, made of people who fail and repair, and the texts themselves tell it, as at Kosambi.

orig.note: Pali sangha: the community, the order of monks and nuns, and in wider use all who follow the path.

carryVoice: Your line: made of people. Even the Buddha's own monks quarreled, and made it up. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: The world does not know that we must all come to an end here;—but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once.
